questions.q: What is the purpose of the kid (Key ID) parameter in a JWT header?
o: It specifies the username who issued the token
It tells the server which key to retrieve for signature verification
It encodes the expiration date in a compact format
It identifies the JWT version number
questions.x: kid is part of the JWT header and is used by the server to look up the correct verification key when multiple keys exist, for example during key rotation. The server trusts this value to locate the right key.
questions.h: Servers can have more than one signing key. kid helps them answer: which key should I use for this specific token?

questions.q: In this lab, where does the server look up the key identified by the kid value?
o: A remote JWKS endpoint on an external CDN
A PostgreSQL database table
The local filesystem at a path derived from the kid value
An in-memory map populated at startup
questions.x: The server appends the kid value to a base directory path and reads a file from disk. This creates a path traversal vulnerability when kid contains ../ sequences.
questions.h: The attack is called path traversal. What type of resource is accessed via a path on a server? Think about what ../ does in a file path.

questions.q: Why is /dev/null the ideal target for this attack?
o: It triggers a kernel panic that disables authentication checks
Reading it returns an empty string, making the effective HMAC secret an empty string the attacker can predict
It exposes the real signing key as an error message
It has world-readable permissions that bypass filesystem ACLs
questions.x: On Linux, /dev/null is a virtual device that always returns zero bytes when read. The server gets an empty string as the key. The attacker signs their forged token with the same empty string, so both sides match.
questions.h: The attacker needs to know the key value that the server will use. What file always has a completely predictable, constant content?

questions.q: What path traversal string navigates from an arbitrary directory to the filesystem root?
o: /root
questions.x: Each ../ goes up one directory. Using many of them in a row guarantees reaching the root regardless of the starting depth. On Linux, going above the root is silently clamped, so too many ../ sequences are harmless.
questions.h: A single ../ goes up one level. If you don't know the starting depth, how many would you use to be sure you reach the root?

questions.q: After pointing kid to /dev/null, what algorithm and secret does the attacker use to sign the forged token?
o: RS256 with a self-generated private key
HS256 with an empty string as the secret
HS512 with the string 'null'
none algorithm with no signature
questions.x: The server uses HS256 and reads the key from /dev/null, getting empty bytes. The attacker therefore signs with HS256 and an empty string. Both parties compute the same HMAC because the key is empty on both sides.
questions.h: The server's key file returns nothing. What value would you use to match a secret that is empty?

questions.q: What tool was used in the writeup to craft and sign the forged JWT?
o: jwt.io browser tool
Python with PyJWT and the cracked secret
hashcat with mode 16500
Burp Suite's Intruder module
questions.x: PyJWT in Python can sign tokens with arbitrary secrets including an empty string. You provide the payload, the algorithm (HS256), and the secret (''), and it produces a valid-looking token.
questions.h: The writeup uses the same Python JWT library found in other JWT labs. Which library starts with PyJ?

questions.q: What makes path traversal in the kid parameter possible at the code level?
o: The JWT library has a known CVE for this exact path
The server concatenates the kid value into a file path without sanitizing or validating it first
kid is an optional header so the server ignores validation for it
The filesystem permissions are misconfigured
questions.x: The vulnerability is unsanitized concatenation. The code does something like: open(base_path + kid). If kid is ../../dev/null, the resulting path escapes the intended directory.
questions.h: The server builds a filesystem path using a value it did not validate. What happens when you concatenate user-controlled input into a path without checking it?

questions.q: Which defensive technique would most directly prevent this attack?
o: Encrypt the JWT so the kid value cannot be read
Validate kid against an allowlist of known key identifiers before using it as a path component
Use RS256 so the key is never read from disk
Rate-limit requests to reduce the number of traversal attempts
questions.x: An allowlist compares the kid value against a set of known, expected identifiers such as UUIDs you generated. Any kid that does not match exactly is rejected before any filesystem access occurs.
questions.h: The server should not accept any kid value it was not expecting. What validation pattern rejects anything not on a pre-approved list?

questions.q: Which of these kid values would an allowlist correctly reject?
o: prod-primary
rsa-v2
questions.x: The traversal string is clearly not a valid key identifier. A strict allowlist that accepts only known strings like key-2026-01 or prod-primary would reject it immediately.
questions.h: Which option looks like a filesystem traversal attempt rather than a normal key identifier?

questions.q: Why is this attack dangerous even on servers that store keys securely?
o: Secure key storage prevents the attack entirely
The attack bypasses key storage by replacing the key with /dev/null, a value independent of any stored keys
Secure key storage makes the attack harder but not impossible
The attack only works when keys are stored in environment variables
questions.x: The attack does not try to steal the real key. It redirects the key lookup to a file with known, attacker-controlled content. Secure storage of the legitimate key is irrelevant if the lookup mechanism can be hijacked.
questions.h: The attack does not target the stored key at all. It replaces the key path with a file the attacker controls. Does securing the original key stop this substitution?
